content: The Lake Wobegon effect refers to the human tendency to overestimate one’s own achievements and abilities in comparison to others. It also describes the observation that, in many educational tests, a significant majority of participants achieve results above the statistical norm. This phenomenon is named after the fictional town of Lake Wobegon from the radio series A Prairie Home Companion, where the presenter, Garrison Keillor, famously described the town as a place where “all the women are strong, all the men are good-looking, and all the children are above average.” In studies of overconfidence, Swedish researcher Ola Svenson found that 80% of surveyed drivers rated themselves as being in the top 30% of all drivers. Similarly, Zuckerman and Jost (2001) demonstrated that most college students believed themselves to be “more popular than average.” This pattern of self-assessment, where a large majority of individuals claim to be above average, has been observed across various groups, including drivers, CEOs, stock market analysts, college students, police officers, and state education officials. Numerous experiments and surveys have consistently shown that most people believe they possess attributes that are superior or more desirable than average. The term is also used to describe a societal tendency to treat children as “special” to enhance their self-esteem, even when the children may only be average or underperforming. For example, a College Board survey of 829,000 high school seniors revealed that fewer than 1% rated themselves as below average in their ability to “get along with others.” Furthermore, 60% rated themselves in the top 10%, and 25% rated themselves in the top 1%. It has been suggested that subjective traits, such as interpersonal skills, may be more prone to distortion in self-assessment. The Lake Wobegon effect has been repeatedly identified in studies examining other traits, such as fairness, virtuousness, luck, and investing ability. It is conceptually related to phenomena like in-group bias and wishful thinking. In contrast, the “worse-than-average effect” describes a tendency to underestimate one’s abilities in certain contexts, which may involve self-handicapping behaviors. This can also be compared to the false consensus effect. In 1987, John Cannell conducted a study that reported the statistically impossible finding that all U.S. states claimed their average student test scores were above the national norm. While this finding is widely acknowledged, the underlying causes remain debated. In statistical terms, it is not always expected that exactly half of survey participants will score above average and the other half below average. Asymmetric distributions can occur, where the data is skewed. For instance, if one individual in a group scores significantly lower than others, the majority of participants may appear to be above average. For example, if five students rate their appearance on a scale of 1 to 10, and four rate themselves as a 9 while one rates themselves as a 4, the mean score would be 8, making 80% of the students above the “average” score. Similarly, in binary distributions, such as a pass/fail exam, all passing students (scoring 1) would be above average, while all failing students (scoring 0) would be below average. However, such effects of asymmetry in distribution are not typically classified as the Lake Wobegon effect. The Lake Wobegon effect specifically refers to an upward shift in the statistical distribution, rather than an asymmetry.
